criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains the cascading-failure mechanism (shared worker/connection-pool exhaustion, head-of-line blocking) and the amplifying role of naive retries and the oversized timeout, and applies each mitigation with correct semantics: SLO-aligned timeouts, backoff+jitter/retry-budget retries, bulkhead isolation, circuit breaker, and graceful degradation. No technically wrong claims (e.g. that adding workers or raising the timeout resolves the coupling).

Delivers both a diagnosis (why one dependency downed the whole service) and mitigations spanning the required axes — timeout, retry policy, resource isolation, circuit breaking, and fallback/degradation — plus a critique of the teammate's proposal, rather than fixing only one dimension.

Ties each recommendation to its effect on blast radius/availability and surfaces trade-offs (e.g. fail-open vs fail-closed, availability vs answer quality, why more retries/longer timeouts worsen saturation), rather than listing resilience patterns without connecting them to the observed failure.

Reads as a coherent design-review narrative: states the failure mechanism first, then presents organized, prioritized mitigations using correct terminology (cascading failure, bulkhead, circuit breaker, backoff, graceful degradation).

expected_answer_points: Identifies the mechanism as a cascading failure: slow LLM calls hold workers/connections until the long timeout, and because all endpoints share one worker pool, the pool is exhausted and unrelated endpoints starve (head-of-line blocking / resource exhaustion)
Explains that immediate 3x retries amplify the failure — they multiply load on the degraded provider (retry storm) and multiply worker-hold time per request

Argues the teammate's fix is counterproductive: raising the timeout makes stuck workers hold longer (saturating the pool faster), and more retries add more load — both amplify the root cause without touching the shared-resource coupling
Recommends tight, SLO/p99-aligned timeouts (plus an overall deadline) so hung calls fail fast and release workers
Recommends a disciplined retry policy: retry only retryable errors, with exponential backoff + jitter, a small cap, honoring Retry-After, and/or a retry budget
Recommends bulkhead/isolation — a separate bounded pool or concurrency limit for the LLM path so its saturation cannot starve non-LLM endpoints, capping the blast radius
Recommends a circuit breaker that fails fast on sustained errors/latency (with half-open recovery) instead of piling up calls against a down dependency

Recommends graceful degradation / fail-open behavior (retrieval-only answer, cached/templated response, or explicit 'AI unavailable' state) and names a trade-off (e.g. availability vs answer quality, fail-open vs fail-closed)
common_pitfalls: Blames the LLM provider outage and stops there, without explaining the internal amplification (shared pool exhaustion + retry storm) that turned a dependency issue into a full-service outage
Endorses or only mildly tweaks the teammate's fix — treats it as a capacity problem to be solved by more workers, longer timeouts, or more retries, all of which worsen or merely delay pool saturation

Proposes retries without qualification: retrying on all errors (including non-retryable 4xx), with no backoff/jitter, no cap, and no retry budget — which produces a retry storm against a degraded provider
Adds a circuit breaker but no fallback, so users still get hard errors — confusing 'the service stays up' with 'the feature still does something useful' (missing graceful/fail-open degradation)
Omits resource isolation/bulkheading entirely, leaving the shared worker pool as a single point of coupling so any one slow dependency can still starve every endpoint
Sets a timeout but leaves it far larger than the SLO/p99, so hung calls still hold workers long enough to exhaust the pool
reference_answer:
The provider outage is the trigger, but the real defect is that one slow dependency is allowed to consume resources shared by the whole service — a classic cascading failure.

Mechanism: when LLM p99 latency spikes, each `/assist` request holds its worker (thread/async task) and upstream connection until the 60s timeout. The ‘retry 3x immediately’ turns one slow request into up to four sequential slow calls AND adds a retry storm that further overloads the already-degraded provider. Because all endpoints share one worker pool, these long-held workers exhaust the pool; requests to unrelated endpoints can't acquire a worker and 503. That is head-of-line blocking / resource-pool exhaustion through a shared bulkhead.

Why the proposal is wrong: raising the timeout to 120s makes each stuck worker hold longer, so the pool saturates faster and stays saturated longer; two more retries multiply load on the failing provider and burn more worker-time. Both amplify the exact mechanism that caused the outage; neither addresses the shared-resource coupling.

Fixes (prioritized):
1. SLO-aligned timeouts. Replace 60s with a per-attempt timeout near the acceptable p99 (single-digit seconds) plus an overall deadline, so a hung call fails fast and releases the worker.
2. Disciplined retries. Retry only retryable failures (timeouts, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff + jitter, a small cap (1–2), honoring `Retry-After`, governed by a retry budget so retries can't multiply load during an incident.
3. Bulkhead isolation. Give the LLM path its own bounded concurrency limit / thread pool / connection pool so its saturation cannot starve endpoints that don't call the LLM — this caps the blast radius to `/assist`.
4. Circuit breaker. Trip on sustained errors/latency and fail fast (with half-open probes to recover) instead of queuing doomed calls against a dead provider.
5. Graceful degradation. Make the feature fail-open: on LLM failure return retrieval results without synthesis, a cached/templated answer, or an explicit ‘AI temporarily unavailable’ state, so the product keeps working.
6. Detection & shedding. Monitor per-dependency latency/error rate and pool saturation against SLOs/error budgets; add load shedding, and consider moving generation off the request path (queue + `202` + poll) if latency can't be bounded.

Trade-off: fail-open preserves availability but can serve lower-quality answers; tight timeouts may abort some slow-but-valid calls. The net principle is: isolate the dependency, fail fast, degrade gracefully, and make retries safe — so a provider incident degrades one feature instead of the whole service.
